routes.description: Establish that human freedom requires genuine alternative possibilities and agent sourcehood, and that deliberation can embody both without collapsing into deterministic production or uncontrolled randomness.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by connecting deliberative experience to a coherent model of open yet reason-guided choice, locating control in the agent, and explaining how bounded self-formation supports freedom and responsibility despite inherited constraints.

motionBridge.description: Show that freedom in the motion-relevant sense requires agents to originate choices among genuinely available alternatives.

centralBridges.description: Explain why indeterminacy can preserve live alternatives without reducing choice to chaos or mere event-level randomness.
Locate reason-guided control and causal origination in the person rather than solely in antecedent sufficient conditions.
Show how agents can shape character and future possibilities despite biological, social, and environmental constraints.
Justify treating the experienced structure and practical efficacy of deliberation as evidence for sourcehood and alternatives.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish causal production from non-causal entailment so the implications of different forms of determination remain clear.
Establish appropriate limits on claims that current scientific findings have already resolved the metaphysical dispute.

routes.description: Establish that determinism leaves intact practically and normatively important forms of willing, choice, responsibility, consent, and agency without requiring libertarian alternatives or ultimate self-origination.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by identifying responsibility-relevant distinctions preserved under determinism, grounding agency in proximal personal processes and causal feedback, and showing that libertarian alternatives or ultimate sourcehood add no necessary condition for practical agency.

motionBridge.description: Show that meaningful will, responsibility, and practical agency survive determinism without libertarian alternative possibilities or ultimate sourcehood.

centralBridges.description: Specify stable distinctions between willing and unwilling action, consent and compulsion, and choices and nonchoices under determinism.
Ground agency in the person's reasons, character, neural processes, and causal feedback without demanding an ultimately self-caused will.
Test whether indeterminate selection and agent-set criteria actually provide the alternatives and authorship claimed for libertarian freedom.
Explain responsibility through the practical functions of praise, blame, prediction, and interpersonal regulation rather than a single metaphysical condition.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Separate non-causal determination from external forcing and clarify why predictability alone does not displace personal agency.
Account for the tension between first-person deliberation and deterministic self-description without treating it as sufficient to establish libertarianism.

sections.title: Deliberation, Indeterminacy, and Genuine Alternatives
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether deliberation can involve genuinely open options under reason-guided constraints or whether indeterministic selection remains randomness-like and unnecessary for agency.

sections.title: Agent Sourcehood and Levels of Causal Control
sections.rationale: The motion centrally turns on whether the person can originate action through agent-level or criterial control, and whether proximal personal causation is sufficient without ultimate sourcehood.

sections.title: Inherited Constraints, Self-Formation, and Responsibility
sections.rationale: This issue tests how genetic, social, and environmental formation bears on authorship, live possibilities, character development, and responsibility across both accounts of freedom.

sections.title: Willing Action, Consent, and Practical Agency
sections.rationale: The compatibilist alternative depends on whether distinctions among choices, reflexes, coercion, consent, and compelled conduct remain meaningful and responsibility-relevant under determinism.

sections.title: Scientific, Pragmatic, and First-Person Grounds
sections.rationale: This supporting issue concerns what neuroscience, deliberative phenomenology, pragmatism, and the tension between inquiry and self-description can establish about either conception of freedom.
